lines.text: Chapter 1: Meet the money bosses.
lines.say: Chapter one: meet the money bosses.

lines.text: A central bank is the bank for a country's banks. It controls the most basic price in money: the cost of borrowing overnight.
lines.say: A central bank is the bank for a country's banks. It controls the most basic price in money: the cost of borrowing overnight.

lines.text: In the US, that's the Federal Reserve, the most-watched central bank of all.
lines.say: In the US, that's the Federal Reserve, the most-watched central bank of all.

lines.text: As of early October 2026, its target for the overnight rate between banks was 3.75% to 4%.
lines.say: As of early October twenty twenty-six, its target for the overnight rate between banks was three point seven five to four percent.

lines.text: Many other rates, from car loans to savings accounts, get built on top of that one.
lines.say: Many other rates, from car loans to savings accounts, get built on top of that one.

lines.text: Five of these banks move markets the most. First, the Fed, which runs the dollar.
lines.say: Five of these banks move markets the most. First, the Fed, which runs the dollar.

lines.text: Second, the European Central Bank in Frankfurt, which runs the euro.
lines.say: Second, the European Central Bank in Frankfurt, which runs the euro.

lines.text: Then the Bank of Japan, for the yen, and the Bank of England, for the pound.
lines.say: Then the Bank of Japan, for the yen, and the Bank of England, for the pound.

lines.text: And the People's Bank of China, founded in 1948, which manages the yuan.
lines.say: And the People's Bank of China, founded in nineteen forty-eight, which manages the yuan.

lines.text: They don't all have the same job. The Fed's goals are written into the Federal Reserve Act.
lines.say: They don't all have the same job. The Fed's goals are written into the Federal Reserve Act: maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.

scene.text: maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates

lines.text: People call it the dual mandate: jobs and prices, with an inflation goal of 2%.
lines.say: People call it the dual mandate: jobs and prices, with an inflation goal of two percent.

lines.text: The ECB has one main job: price stability, which it defines as 2% inflation over the medium term.
lines.say: The E C B has one main job: price stability, which it defines as two percent inflation over the medium term.

lines.text: The Bank of England also aims for 2%, but the UK government sets that target. The bank picks the rate to hit it.
lines.say: The Bank of England also aims for two percent, but the UK government sets that target. The bank picks the rate to hit it.

lines.text: The Bank of Japan has had a 2% price target since 2013.
lines.say: The Bank of Japan has had a two percent price target since twenty thirteen.

lines.text: China's central bank law gives it a different goal: keep the currency's value stable, and thereby promote growth.
lines.say: China's central bank law gives it a different goal: keep the currency's value stable, and thereby promote growth.

scene.text: maintain the stability of the value of the currency and thereby promote economic growth

lines.text: There's another difference. The other four set rates independently. China's central bank works under the leadership of the State Council, China's cabinet.
lines.say: There's another difference. The other four set rates independently. China's central bank works under the leadership of the State Council, China's cabinet.

lines.text: Chapter 2: A short history.
lines.say: Chapter two: a short history.

lines.text: Central banks are older than you'd think. Sweden's Riksbank, from 1668, is the oldest still running.
lines.say: Central banks are older than you'd think. Sweden's Riksbank, from sixteen sixty-eight, is the oldest one still running.

lines.text: The Bank of England followed in 1694, set up to lend money to the government.
lines.say: The Bank of England followed in sixteen ninety-four, set up to lend money to the government.

lines.text: Japan's central bank came in 1882. America's Fed arrived only in 1913, after the bank panic of 1907.
lines.say: Japan's central bank came in eighteen eighty-two. America's Fed arrived only in nineteen thirteen, after the bank panic of nineteen-oh-seven.

lines.text: The ECB is the baby. It opened in 1998, months before the euro launched in 1999.
lines.say: The E C B is the baby. It opened in nineteen ninety-eight, months before the euro launched in nineteen ninety-nine.

lines.text: The basic lever never changed. Raise rates to cool inflation. Cut rates when the economy slumps.
lines.say: The basic lever never changed. Raise rates to cool inflation. Cut rates when the economy slumps.

lines.text: Most famously, around 1980 and 1981, Fed Chair Paul Volcker let the key rate climb to about 20% to break double-digit inflation.
lines.say: Most famously, around nineteen eighty and nineteen eighty-one, Fed Chair Paul Volcker let the key rate climb to about twenty percent to break double-digit inflation.

lines.text: Fast forward. The top of the Fed's range was 1.75% at the end of 2019, then near zero for 2020 and 2021.
lines.say: Fast forward. The top of the Fed's range was one point seven five percent at the end of twenty nineteen, then near zero for twenty twenty and twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: Then came the fastest hikes in decades: 5.50% by the end of 2023, the highest since 2001.
lines.say: Then came the fastest hikes in decades: five and a half percent by the end of twenty twenty-three, the highest since two thousand one.

lines.text: Cuts brought it down to 3.75% by the end of 2025.
lines.say: Cuts brought it down to three point seven five percent by the end of twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Then, on September 16, 2026, the Fed raised it to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first hike since July 2023.
lines.say: Then, on September sixteenth, twenty twenty-six, the Fed raised it to a range of three point seven five to four percent, its first hike since July twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: Japan's story runs the other way. In 2016, after years of weak prices, it pushed its key rate below zero, to minus 0.1%.
lines.say: Japan's story runs the other way. In twenty sixteen, after years of weak prices, it pushed its key rate below zero, to minus zero point one percent.

lines.text: For eight years, banks paid to park money there. Japan was the last central bank to end negative rates, in March 2024.
lines.say: For eight years, banks paid to park money there. Japan was the last central bank to end negative rates, in March twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: Then it climbed: 0.25% in 2024, 0.75% in 2025, 1% in June 2026, and 1.25% in September 2026.
lines.say: Then it climbed: zero point two five percent in twenty twenty-four, zero point seven five in twenty twenty-five, one percent in June twenty twenty-six, and one point two five percent in September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Chapter 3: The 2026 scoreboard.
lines.say: Chapter three: the twenty twenty-six scoreboard.

lines.text: Here's where the big four stood in early October 2026. The Fed: 3.75% to 4%, after its September hike.
lines.say: Here's where the big four stood in early October twenty twenty-six. The Fed: three point seven five to four percent, after its September hike.

lines.text: The euro area: a 2.50% deposit rate, after hikes in June and September 2026, the ECB's first since 2023.
lines.say: The euro area: a two point five percent deposit rate, after hikes in June and September twenty twenty-six, the E C B's first since twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: The UK: 3.75%. The Bank of England held in September 2026, but three of its nine voters wanted a hike.
lines.say: The UK: three point seven five percent. The Bank of England held in September twenty twenty-six, but three of its nine voters wanted a hike.

lines.text: Japan: 1.25%, the lowest of the four, after six hikes starting in March 2024.
lines.say: Japan: one point two five percent, the lowest of the four, after six hikes starting in March twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: China works differently. Its main policy rate, the 7-day reverse repo rate, was 1.40% in early October, unchanged since May 2025.
lines.say: China works differently. Its main policy rate, the seven-day reverse repo rate, was one point four percent in early October, unchanged since May twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: In September, Chinese banks priced loans off loan prime rates of 3.0% for one year and 3.5% for five years.
lines.say: In September, Chinese banks priced loans off loan prime rates of three percent for one year, and three and a half percent for five years.

lines.text: Both were unchanged for 16 months in a row through September 2026. While three big banks hiked, China held still.
lines.say: Both were unchanged for sixteen months in a row through September twenty twenty-six. While three big banks hiked, China held still.

lines.text: Why all the hikes? Largely, energy. After the Iran war began in late February 2026, oil jumped.
lines.say: Why all the hikes? Largely, energy. After the Iran war began in late February twenty twenty-six, oil jumped.

lines.text: Brent crude closed at $105.28 a barrel on September 28, 2026.
lines.say: Brent crude closed at about a hundred and five dollars a barrel on September twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Prices followed. In August 2026, US inflation was 3.4%, UK inflation 3.1%, and euro-area inflation above 3%.
lines.say: Prices followed. In August twenty twenty-six, US inflation was three point four percent, UK inflation three point one, and euro-area inflation above three.

lines.text: And every one of those banks is aiming for 2%. That gap is what they're fighting.
lines.say: And every one of those banks is aiming for two percent. That gap is what they're fighting.

lines.text: Rates are one tool. The other is the balance sheet: bonds a central bank buys with money it creates.
lines.say: Rates are one tool. The other is the balance sheet: bonds a central bank buys with money it creates.

lines.text: On September 23, 2026, the Fed held about $6.7 trillion in assets, down from about $9 trillion in 2022.
lines.say: On September twenty-third, twenty twenty-six, the Fed held about six point seven trillion dollars in assets, down from about nine trillion in twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: The Eurosystem held about €6.1 trillion in June 2026, down from €8.8 trillion at its 2022 peak.
lines.say: The euro system held about six point one trillion euros in June twenty twenty-six, down from eight point eight trillion at its twenty twenty-two peak.

lines.text: The Bank of Japan held about 662 trillion yen at the end of March 2026, down 9.3% in a year.
lines.say: The Bank of Japan held about six hundred sixty-two trillion yen at the end of March twenty twenty-six, down nine point three percent in a year.

lines.text: Here's the jaw-dropper. By March 2023, Japan's central bank owned about 53% of all Japanese government bonds.
lines.say: Here's the jaw-dropper. By March twenty twenty-three, Japan's central bank owned about fifty-three percent of all Japanese government bonds.

lines.text: Its share only dipped below half in March 2026, as it buys fewer bonds.
lines.say: Its share only dipped below half in March twenty twenty-six, as it buys fewer bonds.

lines.text: Chapter 4: How one bank shakes markets.
lines.say: Chapter four: how one bank shakes markets.

lines.text: Central banks move more than their own countries, because money flows toward wherever it earns more.
lines.say: Central banks move more than their own countries, because money flows toward wherever it earns more.

lines.text: Take 2024. Investors had borrowed cheap yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad. It's called the carry trade.
lines.say: Take twenty twenty-four. Investors had borrowed cheap yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad. It's called the carry trade.

lines.text: Then, on July 31, 2024, Japan raised rates. The yen jumped, and many traders rushed to unwind those bets.
lines.say: Then, on July thirty-first, twenty twenty-four, Japan raised rates. The yen jumped, and many traders rushed to unwind those bets.

lines.text: Add a weak US jobs report, and on August 5, 2024, Japan's Nikkei fell 12.4%, its worst day since 1987.
lines.say: Add a weak US jobs report, and on August fifth, twenty twenty-four, Japan's Nikkei fell twelve point four percent, its worst day since nineteen eighty-seven.

lines.text: The Dow dropped about 1,000 points that day. A move in Tokyo hit New York.
lines.say: The Dow dropped about a thousand points that day. A move in Tokyo hit New York.

lines.text: Still, the Fed is the biggest mover of all, because the dollar is on one side of 89% of all currency trades.
lines.say: Still, the Fed is the biggest mover of all, because the dollar is on one side of eighty-nine percent of all currency trades.

lines.text: When US rates rise, dollar savings pay more, so global money tends to move toward the dollar.
lines.say: When US rates rise, dollar savings pay more, so global money tends to move toward the dollar.

lines.text: In September 2026, the dollar index rose nearly 2%, its best month since June.
lines.say: In September twenty twenty-six, the dollar index rose nearly two percent, its best month since June.

lines.text: It shows up in long-term borrowing costs, too. The 10-year Treasury yield ended September 2026 at 5.29%, around its highest since 2002.
lines.say: It shows up in long-term borrowing costs, too. The ten-year Treasury yield ended September twenty twenty-six at five point two nine percent, around its highest since two thousand two.

lines.text: And the other banks watch the Fed. When US rates rise faster, their currencies can weaken, and imports get pricier.
lines.say: And the other banks watch the Fed. When US rates rise faster, their currencies can weaken, and imports get pricier.

lines.text: That was part of Japan's worry in September 2026: with the yen near 157 per dollar, imports like oil cost more.

lines.text: Chapter 5: How it reaches your wallet.
lines.say: Chapter five: how it reaches your wallet.

lines.text: So how does all this reach you? Through three main pipes. Pipe one is mortgages.
lines.say: So how does all this reach you? Through three main pipes. Pipe one is mortgages.

lines.say: On October first, twenty twenty-six, the average thirty-year fixed rate was seven point two eight percent. A year earlier, it was six point three four percent.

lines.text: Example: a $400,000, 30-year loan. At 6.34%, that's about $2,486 a month. At 7.28%, about $2,737.
lines.say: Example: a four hundred thousand dollar, thirty-year loan. At six point three four percent, that's about two thousand four hundred eighty-six dollars a month. At seven point two eight percent, about two thousand seven hundred thirty-seven.

lines.say: That's about two hundred fifty-one dollars more every month, or about three thousand dollars a year.

lines.say: Over all three hundred sixty payments, that's about ninety thousand dollars more in interest.

lines.say: Same house, same price. The difference came from rates, set in part by central banks and global bond markets.

lines.text: Pipe two is savings. In late September 2026, after the Fed's hike, top savings accounts advertised about 4.25% APY.
lines.say: Pipe two is savings. In late September twenty twenty-six, after the Fed's hike, top savings accounts advertised about four and a quarter percent A P Y.

lines.text: For example, $10,000 earning 4.25% for a year makes about $425 in interest.
lines.say: For example, ten thousand dollars earning four and a quarter percent for a year makes about four hundred twenty-five dollars in interest.

lines.text: So higher rates cut both ways. Borrowers pay more, and savers earn more.
lines.say: So higher rates cut both ways. Borrowers pay more, and savers earn more.

lines.text: Pipe three is the dollar. Higher US rates tend to pull money into dollars and make the dollar stronger.
lines.say: Pipe three is the dollar. Higher US rates tend to pull money into dollars and make the dollar stronger.

lines.text: A stronger dollar makes foreign trips and imported goods cheaper for Americans, but makes US exports pricier abroad.
lines.say: A stronger dollar makes foreign trips and imported goods cheaper for Americans, but makes US exports pricier abroad.

lines.text: It can also work in reverse. When Japan or Europe raises rates, their currencies can strengthen, and that trip costs you more.

post.title: Three giant central banks hiked within nine days in Sept. 2026. Who really moves markets?
post.ig: Three giant central banks raised rates within nine days in September 2026. Here's who moves markets, and how it reaches your wallet.

post.yt_desc:
Three giant central banks raised rates within nine days in September 2026: the ECB (deposit rate 2.50%), the Fed (3.75%-4.00%) and the Bank of Japan (1.25%, its highest since 1995), while the Bank of England held at 3.75% and China held its loan prime rates. This video explains what central banks do, their mandates and history, how Japan went from negative rates to 1.25%, how a Bank of Japan hike helped rattle markets in August 2024, and how rate moves reach American wallets through mortgages, savings yields and the dollar, with a worked example on a hypothetical $400,000 mortgage at 6.34% versus 7.28% (about $251 more a month). All rates are as of early October 2026. The Fed, ECB, Bank of Japan and Bank of England met again between October 28 and November 5, 2026, after this video's data cutoff; check their latest decisions.
